name: Giddings-Strominger Wormhole
description: A space of four dimensions and no time, Steven B. Giddings and Andrew Strominger's axion wormhole of 1988: two regions of flat space joined at a throat, a 3-sphere of radius $a$ held open by the field strength of an axion. Cut in half at the throat, it describes a closed baby universe budding off flat space.
convention: The length $a$ is the radius of the throat and the space's only parameter. All four coordinates are spatial, so no component carries a factor of $c$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to arc length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history:
Four dimensions of space and none of time make up this geometry, $$ds^2 =  rac{dr^2}{1 - a^4/r^4} + r^2\,d\Omega_3^2,$$ where $d\Omega_3^2$ is the round metric of the unit 3-sphere and each value of $r$ labels a 3-sphere of radius $r$ [hebecker2018]. The 3-spheres shrink to a smallest one of radius $a$, the throat, and open out again beyond it, joining two asymptotically flat regions of four dimensions [giddings1988, hebecker2018]. An axion's field strength $H$, a 3-form, threads every 3-sphere with the same flux and holds the throat open [giddings1988]. The curvature scalar is $R = -6a^4/r^6$, and the Einstein tensor, which carries the field's stress, has $G^r{}_r = -3a^4/r^6$ along the radius and $3a^4/r^6$ along each direction on the sphere. Embedded in flat space of three dimensions, a slice through the throat makes a funnel whose two sheets level off at a height $\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(1/4)\,a/(4\Gamma(3/4)) \approx 1.311a$ above and below it. ¶ Steven B. Giddings and Andrew Strominger published the solution in 1988, coupling the axion to gravity through a rank three antisymmetric tensor field strength [giddings1988]. They showed that an instanton changing the topology of an asymptotically flat space needs a Ricci tensor with a negative eigenvalue somewhere [giddings1988]. An ordinary real scalar field with a positive kinetic term has $R_{\mu
u} = 
abla_\mu\phi
abla_
u\phi$ and no negative eigenvalue [giddings1988]. For the axion in the 3-form description, the Euclidean stress has the opposite sign, and the Ricci eigenvalues are nonpositive [giddings1988]. Giddings and Strominger also found that a massless dilaton can suppress tunnelling for the couplings in the string effective action they studied [giddings1988]. The axion charge $n$ carried through the throat fixes its radius ($a^2 \propto |n|$); the gravitational semiclassical approximation requires $a$ to be much larger than the Planck length [giddings1988, witten2026]. ¶ Giddings and Strominger cut the space in half through the throat, where the 3-sphere is a minimal surface [giddings1988]. Each half represents tunnelling from flat space $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$ together with a separate 3-sphere, a closed baby universe [giddings1988]. The minimal 3-sphere has no extrinsic curvature and $H$ lies along it, so the fields continue to real time as a closed Robertson-Walker universe of radius $a$, created "at its moment of time symmetry and maximal radius" [giddings1988]. The baby universe carries off $n$ units of axion charge, and an observer left in $\mathbb{R}^3$ measures the charge change by $-n$ [giddings1988]. ¶ George V. Lavrelashvili and coauthors had argued in 1987 that quantum coherence may be lost when closed universes of Planck size split off flat space, and bounded the rate of such splitting from the oscillations of neutral kaons [lavrelashvili1987]. Stephen Hawking drew the same conclusion in 1988: an observer in the flat region cannot measure the state of the closed universes that branch off, so "the final state would appear to be a mixed quantum state" [hawking1988]. Giddings and Strominger estimated the effect on kaons in a gas of their instantons and found that it "can be large" for certain baby universe states unless a small parameter suppresses the instantons [giddings1988]. Sidney Coleman found within the year that the wormholes add only local interactions, with coefficients that are operators on the baby universes, so that an observer within one eigenstate sector reads their eigenvalues as constants of nature and sees no loss of coherence [coleman_redherrings1988, coleman1988, hebecker2018]. Giddings and Strominger implemented this sector description with their axion instantons later that year and found that repeated measurements determine the otherwise unknown couplings [gscoherence1988]. An observer who repeats the experiment sees correlations between successive outcomes, with a diminishing increase in entropy per experiment [gscoherence1988]. ¶ Kimyeong Lee derived a cosine potential for the Goldstone boson in 1988 by coupling a complex scalar to gravity and selecting a baby universe eigenstate [lee1988]. Coleman went on to argue that "if wormholes exist, they have the effect of making the cosmological constant vanish" [coleman1988]. Coleman argued that the wave function of the universe with the no-boundary condition of James Hartle and Hawking peaks like a delta function where the cosmological constant is zero, driven by an infrared divergence as the otherwise disconnected universe grows without bound [coleman1988]. Coleman called the theory "doubly a house built on sand", since it rests on wormhole dynamics and on the Euclidean formulation of quantum gravity [coleman1988]. Igor Klebanov, Leonard Susskind, and Tom Banks examined this prescription in a 1988 preprint published in 1989 and found that its result depends on the contour used for the scale factor [klebanov1989]. Their low energy calculation also drives the pion mass to zero, and they argued that wormholes of larger size can invalidate the dilute approximation [klebanov1989]. ¶ Willy Fischler and Leonard Susskind argued in 1989 that the same Euclidean weighting drives wormholes of increasing size toward close packing, violating the assumption of a dilute gas of small wormholes [fischler1989catastrophe]. Giddings and Strominger described interacting universes through third quantization in 1989, with fields that create and annihilate whole universes [giddings_third1989]. They derived an equation for the axion potential at large distances in a semiclassical model, with a minimum at zero effective cosmological constant and a dependence on the unresolved sign of the Euclidean action [giddings_third1989]. Jonathan J. Halliwell and Raymond Laflamme found a wormhole held open by a conformally coupled scalar field in 1989, its 3-spheres growing as $\sqrt{R_0^2 + 	au^2}$ with the distance $	au$ from a throat of radius $R_0$, "a much simpler analytic form" [halliwell1989]. The effective gravitational constant can become negative in this geometry [halliwell1989]. ¶ Laurence F. Abbott and Mark B. Wise allowed the radial scalar to vary in 1989 and obtained wormholes with both broken and unbroken global symmetry [abbott1989]. In the unbroken theory, the action diverges at large radius; the same divergence occurs in the effective theory, leaving finite coefficients for operators that violate the charge [abbott1989]. Giddings and Strominger constructed a string compactification with a radial axion later in 1989, obtaining the same four dimensional wormhole metric and a radial dilaton that diverges only at infinity [string1989]. They inferred effective operators by matching at a finite radius, with unresolved infrared behaviour for a gas of these wormholes [string1989]. ¶ Coleman and Lee derived scalar and flux descriptions of fixed charge amplitudes in 1990, including the boundary terms required to pass between them [colemanlee1990]. They constructed wormholes supported by a massive complex scalar; small wormholes approach the Giddings-Strominger metric, and matching to local operators removes the infrared divergence from the effective couplings [colemanlee1990]. Stuart Alexander Ridgway imposed a boundary at a finite 3-sphere in 1991 and found a regime where operators that violate axion charge become weak [ridgway1991]. ¶ Renata Kallosh and coauthors allowed the radial part of a complex scalar to vary in 1995 and found much smaller wormhole actions; the suppression of charge violation depends on the physics near the Planck scale [kallosh1995]. Valery A. Rubakov and Oleg Yu. Shvedov found a negative homogeneous mode around the axion wormhole in 1996 after rotating the conformal perturbation into the imaginary direction [rubakov1996]. Hongsu Kim solved the Wheeler-DeWitt equation for the axion model in a 1997 preprint published in 1998 [hongsu1998]. The state is regular at zero radius and decays at large radius for a chosen operator ordering within the homogeneous reduction [hongsu1998]. Michael Gutperle and Wafic A. Sabra determined the critical dilaton coupling for regular axion wormholes in arbitrary dimension in 2002; the uncoupled axion limit recovers the Giddings-Strominger geometry [gutperle2002]. ¶ Jin Young Kim, Yoonbai Kim, and James Edward Hetrick found unstable homogeneous harmonic perturbations for a selected string dilaton coupling in 2003 [kim2003]. Eric A. Bergshoeff and coauthors classified the solutions with an axion and a dilaton by their conserved charges in 2004, with regular wormholes below a critical dilaton coupling [nonextremal2004]. They constructed regular solutions of the universal hypermultiplet in four dimensions in a December 2004 preprint published in 2005, supported by a dilaton and a scalar from a Ramond-Ramond field [bergshoeff2005]. Nima Arkani-Hamed, Jacopo Orgera, and Joseph Polchinski constructed regular solutions with several axions in four and six dimensions in 2007 [arkani2007]. An axion wormhole in their six dimensional string compactification connects two boundaries whose field theory amplitudes should factorize, creating a conflict if the saddle contributes [arkani2007]. ¶ Marco Chiodaroli and Gutperle constructed regular wormholes with several axion charges in a 2008 preprint published in 2009 [chiodaroli2009uh]. The shift charges form a Heisenberg algebra, so only commuting sets of charges can be specified at the boundaries [chiodaroli2009uh]. They extended the construction to two hypermultiplets in 2009, retaining the four dimensional throat geometry and imposing conditions for real saddles with a positive scalar action [chiodaroli2009n2]. Miguel Montero, Angel M. Uranga, and Irene Valenzuela calculated higher harmonics in the axion potential in 2015 and argued that gravitational instantons can obstruct inflation over a range larger than the Planck scale [montero2015]. Discrete gauge symmetries can forbid some instantons when several axions are present, changing the allowed harmonics of the potential [montero2015]. ¶ Arthur Hebecker and coauthors calculated the wormhole contribution to an axion potential in 2017 and compared it with the potential needed for inflation [hebecker2017]. They found no strong constraint independent of the microscopic theory from the gravitational instantons under control in their effective theory in four dimensions [hebecker2017]. Arthur Hebecker, Thomas Mikhail and Pablo Soler reviewed the subject in 2018, recording that such wormholes exist in the Euclidean supergravity theories that come from string theory and that a dilute gas of them can break the axion's shift symmetry and give it a potential [hebecker2018]. ¶ Rodrigo Alonso and Alfredo Urbano enforced charge conservation in 2019 and found no physical homogeneous perturbations of the pure axion wormhole [alonso2019]. They also calculated wormhole contributions to axion masses and examined their consequences for the QCD axion, black hole superradiance, and ultralight dark matter, conditional on the validity of Einstein gravity at the throat scale [alonso2019]. Thomas Hertog, Brecht Truijen and Thomas Van Riet found in 2019 perturbations concentrated in the neck that lower the action [hertog2019]. James Alvey and Miguel Escudero calculated wormhole actions for one or several complex scalars in 2021 and found that radial fields can make the violation of global symmetries too large for the QCD axion [alvey2021]. ¶ Gregory J. Loges, Gary Shiu and Nidhi Sudhir, holding the 3-form fixed at the boundary, found in 2022 "a perturbatively stable Euclidean saddle" [loges2022]. The homogeneous perturbations carry no physical degree of freedom at fixed charge, and the constrained homogeneous action has no conformal factor instability [alonso2019, loges2022]. Stefano Andriolo and coauthors calculated corrections from a massive dilaton in 2022, finding a smaller throat and a lower action per unit charge for smaller wormholes in their effective theory [andriolo2022]. Koichi Hamaguchi, Yoshiki Kanazawa, and Natsumi Nagata found in 2022 that a nonminimal coupling of the complex scalar to curvature can increase the wormhole action and suppress the violation of axion charge [hamaguchi2022]. ¶ Dhong Yeon Cheong and coauthors repeated that calculation with an independent connection in 2023; the metric and Palatini formulations approach the same Giddings-Strominger solution when the radial field decouples [cheong2023]. Loges, Shiu, and Van Riet lifted regular four dimensional wormholes supported by axions and dilatons to type IIA supergravity on a 6-torus in 2023 [loges2023lift]. By choosing the charges and integration constants, they kept the string coupling weak and the curvature small throughout the ten dimensional solution [loges2023lift]. Caroline Jonas, George Lavrelashvili, and Jean-Luc Lehners found additional branches in 2023 with oscillations of the dilaton and the 3-sphere radius, including geometries that continue to expanding baby universes [jonas2023]. Alvey and Escudero amended their dilaton action in 2023; its dependence on the effective axion decay constant is logarithmic, which weakens the suppression of symmetry breaking in the model [alvey2023erratum]. Philippe Brax, Clifford P. Burgess, and Fernando Quevedo generated scalar profiles along geodesics in field space in a 2023 preprint published in 2024, retaining the Giddings-Strominger metric for nonlinear sigma models with several fields [brax2024]. ¶ Kanazawa added a term quadratic in the curvature scalar in 2024 and compared the metric and Palatini formulations of gravity [kanazawa2024]. The wormhole action changes little in the metric formulation and decreases at large positive coupling in the Palatini formulation, subject to the cutoff of the effective theory [kanazawa2024]. Jonas, Lavrelashvili, and Lehners tested homogeneous perturbations in 2024 and found stable branches with the smallest initial dilaton potential; other branches have negative modes or enter a range where the perturbation analysis is inconclusive [jonas2024]. Cheong, Seong Chan Park, and Chang Sub Shin separated the contribution near the throat from the contribution at large radius in 2024, allowing them to calculate axion wormhole actions from the scalar kinetic functions [cheong2024]. Luca Martucci, Nicolò Risso, Alessandro Valenti, and Luca Vecchi constructed families with several axions and their scalar partners, the saxions, in 2024 and found exponential suppression of wormhole effects as the number of fields increases, within their supersymmetric axiverse and its range of validity [axiverse2024]. ¶ Hertog, Simon Maenaut, Bruno Missoni, Rob Tielemans, and Van Riet found stable wormholes with axions and saxions in 2024, with agreement between the scalar and 2-form descriptions when both impose fixed axion charge at infinity [hertog2024]. They traced the negative modes of the 2019 calculation to a boundary condition that does not preserve that charge [hertog2024]. The constrained homogeneous fluctuations have a positive action under the physical boundary condition [hertog2024]. Cheong and coauthors used the wormhole potential as the sole source of an axion mass in 2025 and found dark matter parameter ranges consistent with their production and isocurvature constraints [alp2025]. ¶ Donald Marolf and Missoni restored modes even under reflection through the throat in 2025 and found finite positive actions for them, preserving perturbative stability [marolf2025]. Guo-He Li and coauthors obtained oscillating wormholes with an axion and a massive dilaton in a 2025 preprint published in 2026, adding a term proportional to the trace of the stress tensor to the gravitational action [frt2026]. The action increases with the additional coupling along their basic branch; extra oscillations can lower it on other branches for the parameter sets studied [frt2026]. Stephon Alexander and coauthors applied a wormhole potential to an axion coupled to the gravitational Pontryagin density in a 2025 preprint published in 2026, obtaining conditional dark matter and dark energy scenarios [cosmology2026]. ¶ Edward Witten traced the difference to scaling in 2026: with the metric scaled by a constant, the curvature term and the 3-form's term of the action "scale oppositely" and balance at a throat of definite size; a scalar's term scales as the curvature's does, so no balance is possible [witten2026]. To Witten, writing in 2026, it is "the prototype of a Euclidean wormhole solution of Einstein gravity coupled to matter", and in the language of the scalar dual to its 2-form the throat has no semiclassical description [witten2026]. Witten recovered the scalar amplitude by a Poisson resummation of the quantized flux sectors [witten2026]. ¶ Juan Maldacena, Alexander Maloney, and Brian McPeak conjectured a finite bound on displacement in the imaginary direction of axion field space in May 2026, where the sum over wormhole fluxes diverges [maldacena2026]. They argued that a theory valid at shorter distances must invalidate the axion effective theory before that divergence when the wormhole saddle contributes to the path integral [maldacena2026]. Gabriele Di Ubaldo and coauthors obtained a bound of the axionic Weak Gravity Conjecture from positivity of the gravitational path integral in May 2026 [diubaldo2026]. They assumed that wormholes with more asymptotic boundaries are subleading and that the axion wormhole contributes; sufficiently strong instanton effects must then enter before the wormhole sum violates positivity [diubaldo2026]. Muldrow Etheredge and coauthors derived stronger bounds for supersymmetric instantons later that month and checked the conjectured bound in several string compactifications; an instanton remains one possible mechanism for curing the wormhole divergence [etheredge2026]. ¶ Daniele Licciardello and Martucci applied the conjectured imaginary distance bound to noninvertible axion shift symmetries in June 2026; in their supersymmetric axiverse, they argued for towers of instantons that generate a superpotential [imaginary2026]. Kiyoharu Kawana examined the ensemble of baby universe sectors in July 2026 and found localization at a point that preserves the symmetry for the matter vacuum structure assumed in the calculation [kawana2026]. The potential in a specified sector depends on the baby universe state [kawana2026]. ¶ Amin Rezaei Akbarieh separated the axion mass in a specified sector from the spectral gap after averaging over sectors in September 2026 [akbarieh2026]. For a positive normalized measure on a common background, the averaged gap reaches zero when the measure has support arbitrarily close to sectors with zero mass, even if almost every sector has a positive mass [akbarieh2026]. Shubhashis Mallik, Neha, and Gaurav Narain studied fixed axion charge with several metric boundary conditions in September 2026 [mallik2026]. Within their reduction to homogeneous fields and a positive real lapse contour, the wormhole saddle joining opposite sides of the throat has zero intersection number with the contour and contributes no amplitude [mallik2026]. ¶ Shonosuke Takeshita and Naoki Yoshioka allowed torsion and nonmetricity in September 2026 and found that nonminimal couplings to Holst and Nieh-Yan terms can increase the wormhole action [affine2026]. They identified parameter regions that suppress the violation of axion charge; the cutoff for perturbative unitarity remains undetermined in that calculation [affine2026]. Alex Kehagias and Antonio Riotto added a linear coupling between a scalar and Gauss-Bonnet curvature later that month and continued the Einstein wormhole to a complex saddle [gb2026]. At fixed coupling, the corrections that depend on the throat size vanish for large asymptotically flat wormholes, leaving the conjectured imaginary distance threshold unchanged [gb2026]. ¶ Puxin Lin and Shiu calculated a nonperturbative fragmentation channel later that month, in which charged defects lower the action when their charge and tension satisfy the axionic Weak Gravity Conjecture bound [linshiu2026]. The defects split the flux between wormhole segments and leave the local spectrum of small perturbations distinct from this nonperturbative decay channel [linshiu2026]. Soo-Jong Rey calculated the response between two boundaries near a supersymmetric endpoint in October 2026, using a product model with axions and dilatons whose four dimensional metric has the Giddings-Strominger form [rey2026]. The response depends on the imposed charge, scalar boundary data, and state at the boundary; a random matrix description requires additional microscopic assumptions [rey2026].

related.text: The wormhole with a time that Homer Ellis and Kirill Bronnikov found in 1973, its throat held open by a phantom scalar field [ellis1973, bronnikov1973]. Embedded in flat space, a slice through its throat climbs as $\ell\,\mathrm{arccosh}(r/\ell)$, with $\ell$ its throat radius, and never levels off.

With redshift function $\Phi = 0$ and shape function $b = a^4/r^3$, Michael Morris and Kip Thorne's wormhole has at each moment the radial profile of this space, $dr^2/(1 - a^4/r^4)$, with 2-spheres for its 3-spheres, and the same embedding diagram. Its throat needs matter whose tension exceeds its energy density [morris1988].

The closed Friedmann universe with the energy of an axion's field in it, continued to imaginary time, is this space [giddings1988]. Cut at the throat, this space continues back to that universe at radius $a$, "created at its moment of time symmetry and maximal radius" [giddings1988].

The spaces of four dimensions with no time that Stephen Hawking defined as gravitational instantons in 1977, smooth solutions of Einstein's equations without matter [hawking1977]. Giddings and Strominger drew their wormhole, which has an axion's field in it, as "a gravitational instanton with two asymptotically Euclidean regions" [giddings1988].
Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen's bridge of 1935, two sheets of space joined at a smallest sphere, which is a horizon [einstein1935].

Another tunnelling described by a Euclidean solution round in four dimensions, a bubble of lower vacuum energy appearing in a false vacuum, which Sidney Coleman and Frank De Luccia worked out with gravity in 1980 [coleman1980]. Coleman turned to these wormholes in 1988 and argued that they make the cosmological constant vanish [coleman1988].

A gravitational instanton given a time: Euclidean Taub-NUT space with $-c^2dt^2$ added, a static vacuum of five dimensions that four dimensions see as a magnetic monopole [sorkin1983, grossperry1983].

coordinates.name: Areal Radius
domains: r = a \;\text{(the throat, where the two halves meet)}

parameters.description: Radius of the throat, the smallest 3-sphere, a length

coordinates.convention: We use the areal radius $r$, a length, and angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ on the 3-sphere of radius $r$. The chart covers one half of the wormhole, and the other half is its copy glued on at $r = a$.

coordinates.name: Proper Distance (Giddings-Strominger)

parameters.description: Radius of the throat, the smallest 3-sphere, a length
Areal radius, a length, the radius of the 3-sphere at the proper distance $\rho$ from the throat; on the wormhole it solves $(\partial_\rho r)^2 = 1 - a^4/r^4$ with $r(0) = a$

coordinates.convention: We use the proper distance $\rho$ from the throat, a length, negative on the far half, and angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ on the 3-sphere of radius $r$. The radius $r$ is a free function of $\rho$, and no component assumes the equation $(\partial_\rho r)^2 = 1 - a^4/r^4$, whose solution with $r(0) = a$ is the wormhole.
geodesics: \ddot{\rho} - r\,\partial_\rho r\,\dot{\chi}^2 - r\,\partial_\rho r\,\sin^2\chi\,\dot{\theta}^2 - r\,\partial_\rho r\,\sin^2\chi\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Conformal (Loges-Shiu-Sudhir)

parameters.description: Radius of the throat, the smallest 3-sphere, a length

coordinates.convention: We use the pure number $\eta$, negative on the far half, and angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ on the 3-sphere of radius $r$, with $r^2 = a^2\cosh(2\eta)$.
